pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/ˈa.la.lu/** — ​Hittite/Hurrian Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **A-** ​— Open ‌vowel [a] ​— the ​first syllable ‌is light, ​as befits ‌a name ​whose origin ‌remains unknown.
- ​**-la-** — ​Lateral [l] ​between two ​open vowels, ​the liquid ‌center ​that carries ‌the name.
- ​**-lu** — ‌Final open ​syllable with ‌rounded back ​vowel [u], ‌closing the ​name on ​a soft ‌resonance.

For ‌the modern ‌speaker, the ​closest approximation ​is: 'AH-lah-loo' ‌— three ​even syllables; ​the Hittite/Hurrian ‌original is ​irrecoverable, so ​the reconstruction ‌is ​conservative.

Kindred ‌and historical ​forms of ​the name:

- ​**Hittite** — ​Alalu, the ‌first king ‌of the ​gods in ‌the 'Kingship ​in Heaven' ​myth (CTH ‌344)
- **Hurrian** ‌— Alaluwa, ‌the Hurrian ‌form underlying ​the Hittite ‌rendering
- **Cuneiform** ​— 𒀭𒀀𒆷𒇻 ​(a-la-lu), written ​with the ‌divine ​determinative dingir

​Alalu keeps ​its restoration ‌plain: the ​restored form ​Alalu preserves ​only the ‌capital A ​and the ‌Latin alphabet; ​it carries ‌no distinctive ​diacritic or ‌non-ASCII letter. ‌The name's ​Hittite/Hurrian pronunciation ​is unknown, ​and the ​plain form ‌is the ‌most defensible ​display.

domains.body:
**Alalu** is ​the first king ‌of the ‌gods in Hittite ​and Hurrian mythology, ​the original ​occupant of the ​celestial throne before ​Anu the sky-god ‌and long ​before the storm-god ​Teššub. His reign ‌is narrated in ​the 'Kingship ‌in Heaven' myth, ​a Near Eastern ‌succession story ​that parallels the ​Greek sequence of ​Ouranos, Kronos, and ​Zeus. For ​nine years Alalu ‌rules in heaven; ​then his servant ‌**Anu** rises ​against him, and ‌Alalu flees to ​the dark earth ‌below. The ​kingship he loses ‌becomes the inheritance ​that shapes ​the entire Hittite ‌pantheon.

This temple ‌treats Alalu as ‌the **archetype ​of primordial sovereignty**: ​the ruler whose ‌authority is ​ancient, legitimate, and ​yet destined to ‌be overthrown. He ​is not ​a storm-god or ‌a creator; he ​is the first ‌holder of ​the mandate of ​heaven, the figure ​against whom ​every later king ‌defines himself.[^1]

### The ‌Nine-Year Reign

Alalu ​sits on ‌the throne of ​heaven for a ​fixed term of ‌nine years ‌before Anu s쳮ds ‌him — a ‌precise motif of ​cyclic kingship.

### ‌The Servant Who ​S쳮ded

Anu is ​Alalu's servant; ​his rise reverses ‌the social order ​and begins the ​succession that ​leads to Kumarbi ‌and Teššub.

### The ​Dark Earth ​Below

Defeated, Alalu ​descends to the ‌dark earth — ​not a ‌punishment but the ​place from which ‌older powers watch ​newer gods ‌reign.

### The Storm-God's ‌Ancestry

Through Kumarbi, ​Alalu becomes ​the grandfather of ​Teššub, so the ​defeated first king ‌fathers the ‌line that rules ​the storm.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Alalu ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**Throne** — ​The ​first ‌seat ​of ‌divine ​kingship ‌in ​heaven
- ‌**Nine ​years** ‌— ​The fixed ​term ‌of ‌Alalu's ‌reign ​and ​the ‌cyclic ​rhythm ​of ‌succession
- ​**Dark ​earth** ‌— The ​underworld ‌or ​chthonic ​realm ​to ​which ‌the ‌fallen ​first ‌king ​withdraws
- ​**Divine ‌determinative** — ‌The ‌cuneiform ‌dingir ​(𒀭) ‌that ​marks ​Alalu ​as ‌a ​god ​in ​Hittite texts
- ‌**Succession ​chain** ​— ​Alalu ‌→ ​Anu ‌→ ​Kumarbi ‌→ ​Teššub, ‌the ‌Hittite ​parallel to ​Greek ​Ouranos ​→ ‌Kronos ‌→ ​Zeus

mythology.body:
Alalu's mythology ​is almost entirely contained ‌in the 'Kingship in ‌Heaven' narrative, but that ​single text is enough ​to make him one ​of the most important ​figures in Hittite ​and comparative mythology. He ‌is the beginning of ​the dynasty of heaven.[^1]

### ​The First Reign (Kingship ‌in Heaven)

The Hittite ​'Kingship in Heaven' myth ‌(CTH 344) opens ​with Alalu seated on ‌the throne in heaven. ​He is the first ​to hold kingship among ​the gods, and for ​nine years his ​word is law. The ‌text, translated from a ​Hurrian original, presents kingship ‌not as eternal but ​as a rotating office: ‌even the highest god ​may be replaced ‌when his term is ​fulfilled. Alalu's reign is ‌therefore the prototype of ​legitimate rule, not its ​negation.[^2]

### Anu Rises Against ‌Alalu (Overthrow)

After nine ‌years, Alalu's servant ‌Anu confronts him and ​defeats him. Alalu flees ​'down to the dark ‌earth' — a descent ​that removes him from ​active rule but does ‌not annihilate him. ​Anu then takes the ​kingship and rules in ‌turn for nine years. ​The social inversion is ‌striking: the servant becomes ​the master, and ​the first king becomes ​a chthonic memory. The ​pattern will repeat when ‌Kumarbi, Anu's servant, overthrows ‌Anu in turn.

### Alalu ​in the Dark Earth ‌(Descent)

Alalu's withdrawal ​to the dark earth ​is the Hittite equivalent ‌of the deposed primordial ‌father in other Indo-European ‌and Near Eastern mythologies. ‌Unlike Kronos, who is ​imprisoned in Tartaros, ‌or Tiamat, who is ​killed and divided, Alalu ​simply departs. His continued ​existence below the ordered ‌world gives him the ​quality of an ancestor ​rather than a ​destroyed enemy: he is ‌past power, not present ​chaos.

### From Alalu to ​Teššub (Legacy)

The full ​succession runs Alalu → ‌Anu → Kumarbi ​→ Teššub. Kumarbi, who ‌bites off Anu's genitals ​and becomes pregnant with ‌the storm-god, is the ​son or ally of ‌Alalu; through him the ‌defeated first king ​becomes the ancestor of ​the reigning storm-god. This ​genealogy means that every ​thunderbolt Teššub hurls carries, ‌in the distant background, ‌the memory of Alalu's ​first throne.

hittite-texts.title: Hittite Texts
hittite-texts.body: The ​Hittite 'Kingship ‌in ‌Heaven' ​myth—catalogued as ​CTH ​344, the ​*Song ​of ‌Emergence*—is the ​only ​extended ‌narrative that ​names ‌Alalu as ​the ‌first ​king of ​the ​gods. Preserved ​in ​Hittite ‌copies from ​Boğazköy-Hattusa ‌(principally ​KUB 33.120 ‌and ​its duplicates), ‌the ​text ‌is a ​Hittite ​rendering of ‌a ‌Hurrian ‌original and ​sets ​out ‌a cyclical ​theology ​of divine ‌sovereignty: ​Alalu ​rules heaven ‌for ​nine years ‌before ​being ​deposed by ​his ​servant Anu, ‌who ‌in ​turn falls ‌to ​Kumarbi. ​The myth ‌places ‌Alalu at ‌the ‌head ​of the ‌succession ​Alalu → ​Anu ​→ ‌Kumarbi → ​Teššub, ​making ​the deposed ‌first ​king the ​ancestor ​of ‌the storm-god. ​Other ‌Hittite documents ​do ‌not ​narrate Alalu ‌independently, ‌so ​CTH 344 ​remains ​the decisive ​textual ‌witness ‌for his ​figure.

sources.citation: KUB 33.120 (+) 33.119 — Hittite tablets preserving the myth.
Hoffner, H. A., Hittite Myths, 2nd ed. (1998).

cuneiform-archives.title: Cuneiform Archives
cuneiform-archives.body: Alalu ​appears ‌in ‌the ​cuneiform ​tablets ​recovered ​from ​the ‌royal citadel ​archives ​at ‌Boğazköy-Hattusa, ​the ‌Hittite ​capital ‌on ​the ​Anatolian ​plateau. ​The ​relevant ‌manuscripts ​are ‌written ​in ‌the Hittite ​scribal ‌tradition ​using ‌Sumero-Akkadian ​cuneiform ​signs ‌and ‌carry ‌the ​divine ​determinative ‌*dingir* ​(𒀭) ​before ‌the ​name ​*a-la-lu*. ‌The standard ​modern ‌edition, ​*Kingship ​in ​Heaven* ​(CTH ‌344), ‌depends ​on ‌KUB ​33.120 ​(+) ‌33.119; ‌no ‌independent ‌Hurrian ​manuscript ‌has survived, ​so ​the ​Hittite ‌copies ​are ​the ​sole ‌direct ​material ​evidence. ​These ‌tablets ​show ‌how ​Hittite ‌scholars ​preserved and ‌adapted ‌Hurrian ​theological ​material ​within ​their ‌own ‌imperial ​archive.

sources.citation: KUB 33.120 (+) 33.119 — Hittite tablets preserving the myth.
CTH 344 (Song of Emergence / Kingship in Heaven).
Haas, V., Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994).

syncretism.body:
Alalu ​belongs to ‌a widespread ‌ancient ​Near Eastern ​and Mediterranean ​pattern ​of primordial ​king-gods who ‌are ​overthrown by ​their successors.

‌The ​closest parallel ‌is the ​Greek ‌succession *Ouranos ​→ Kronos ​→ ​Zeus*: Ouranos, ​like Alalu, ​is ‌the first ​sky/celestial ‌ruler who ​is deposed ‌by ​a younger ‌power and ​withdraws ‌from the ​active cosmos. ​The ‌Hittite-Hurrian version, ‌however, makes ‌the ​process explicit ​and contractual: ‌each ​king rules ​for nine ‌years ​before being ​replaced. Roman * ‌Saturnus* ​preserves a ‌memory of ​the ​golden-age king ​deposed by ​Jupiter. ‌In Mesopotamian ‌tradition, the ​succession ‌of divine ​kingship from ​Anu ‌to Enlil ‌and later ‌to ‌Marduk follows ​a comparable ‌logic, ​though Alalu ​himself is ​foreign ‌to Sumerian ​and ​Akkadian sources. ​The name ‌Alalu ​has no ​secure etymology; ​it ‌may be ​Hurrian, Hattic, ‌or ​a substrate ‌survival from ​an ‌earlier Anatolian ‌layer.[^1]

Within ​the ​Hittite tradition, ​closely related ​names ‌in the ‌corpus include ​[[telipinu|Telipinu]].

cultural-legacy.body:
Alalu ​survives ‌chiefly ‌as a ​comparative-mythological ​type: ​the ​first ​king of ‌heaven.

​Modern ​scholars ‌cite ​the ‌'Kingship in ​Heaven' ‌text ​as ​a ​key witness ​for ​the ‌Near ​Eastern ‌background ​of Greek ‌theogony, ​and ‌Alalu ​is ‌regularly compared ​to ​Ouranos ‌and ‌Saturnus. ‌He ​appears in ​encyclopedias ‌of ​mythology ​and ‌in studies ​of ​Hittite ‌religion, ​but ‌has ​little direct ​afterlife ​in ​popular ‌culture ‌— precisely ​because ‌his ​myth ​is ‌about ‌*abdication and ‌memory* ‌rather ​than ‌heroic ​action. For ​PuniCodex, ​Alalu ‌is ​a ​restoration ​of the ‌**origin-point ​of ​kingship**: ​the ‌name that ​marks ‌where ​the ‌mandate ​of ‌heaven begins. ‌The ​name ​still ​means: ​**the throne ‌before ‌the ​throne.**[^1]

sources.citation: KUB 33.120 (+) 33.119 — Hittite tablets preserving the myth.

overview.body:
**Alalu** (*alalu*) ​— Primordial ‌King, Heaven · ‌The first king ​of the ​Hittite gods — ​belongs to ​the Hittite tradition, ​where it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain "Primordial ​King, Heaven". ‌The name means ​"Unknown"[^1].

**Alalu** is ‌the first ​king of the ‌gods in ​Hittite and Hurrian ​mythology, the original ​occupant of ​the celestial throne ​before Anu ‌the sky-god and ​long before the ‌storm-god Teššub. ​His reign is ‌narrated in ​the 'Kingship in ‌Heaven' myth, a ​Near Eastern ‌succession story that ​parallels the ​Greek sequence of ‌Ouranos, Kronos, and ‌Zeus. For ‌nine years Alalu ​rules in ​heaven; then his ‌servant **Anu** rises ​against him, ​and Alalu flees ‌to the ​dark earth below. ​The kingship he ‌loses becomes ​the inheritance that ‌shapes the entire ​Hittite pantheon.

​This temple treats ​Alalu as ​the **archetype of ‌primordial sovereignty**: the ‌ruler whose ​authority is ancient, ‌legitimate, and ​yet destined to ​be overthrown. He ‌is not ‌a storm-god or ‌a creator; ‌he is the ​first holder of ‌the mandate ​of heaven, the ​figure against ​whom every later ‌king defines himself.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the canonical scholarly ​spelling **Alalu** ‌and serves its ​temple at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/alalu/). The ​displayed form is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a description computed ‌from the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ASCII ​form *alalu* ‌contains the same ‌letters: no recovered ​diacritics or ​special encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here is ‌consistent citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Cuneiform ​(Hittite/Hurrian ​cycle) ​as ​**𒀭𒀀𒆷𒇻**. Etymologically ‌it ​means ​"Unknown"[^1].

‌The ​canonical ‌spelling **Alalu** ​matches ‌the ​conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*alalu* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters, ​so ‌no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ​transition ‌is ‌claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ​is ‌to ​fix ​one ‌reviewed reference ​spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and ‌provenance, ​and keep ​the ​original ​evidence ‌visible. ‌The displayed ​form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**a** ​→ ​**A** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ​**l** ​→ ‌**l** — ​Same
- ‌**a** ​→ ‌**a** ​— ‌Same
- **l** ‌→ ​**l** ​— ​Same
- ​**u** → ‌**u** ‌— ​Same

meditation.body:
Alalu matters ​to the modern ‌reader precisely ‌because he did ​nothing heroic. He ​held a ​throne for nine ​years, yielded it ​when his ‌time was done, ​and withdrew into ​the dark ‌earth — and ​for that withdrawal ‌he became the ​patriarch of ‌an entire pantheon. ​In an age ​that treats ​power as something ​to be seized, ​held, and ‌defended to the ​last, Alalu embodies ‌a radically ​older idea: that ‌sovereignty is an ​*office*, not a ‌possession, and ​that legitimacy includes ‌the willingness to ​vacate.

The ​'Kingship in Heaven' ‌text makes this ‌explicit in ‌a way no ​other ancient theogony ​dares. Alalu ‌is not murdered, ​mutilated, or imprisoned; ​he is **succeeded**. ‌His fall ​is written into ​the order of ‌things — ​a cosmic constitution ‌in which every ​reign has ​a term, and ​every successor was ​once a servant ‌standing in ‌the courtier's posture, ​cup in hand. ‌Revolution, the ​text says, is ​not the breakdown ‌of order ‌but its deep ‌structure.

And there ‌is a ​quieter lesson in ‌the dark earth ​below. Alalu does ​not vanish ​when defeated; he ‌endures, remembered, ancestral, ​the name ​from which the ​storm-god's whole lineage ‌descends. He ​asks us to ​consider what becomes ​of leaders ‌who learn to ​**retire** — and ‌of cultures that ​know how ‌to retire them. ​Perhaps a mandate ‌is only ‌truly legitimate if ​it can imagine ​its own ​end: the throne ​is sacred because ‌it will ‌one day hold ​someone else.[^1]
